content.content: An inverse of a change-level operation — a creation's or a removal's — is the operation revert of the entries the marker kept. A change's content is never re-derived to take one: no inverse is produced by rebuilding, recomputing or re-committing the affected change's content, and none is drawn from the subject's present content or from its node's text. A recording's inverse is not re-opened here; it is that recording's journal entry (D8c, `kmmowvkw`), a content-side apply. The rule fixes where a change-level inverse comes from: it leaves what a whole-operation inverse restores to D8a (`prsoxsuo`) and the redo side's mechanism to D15b (`qwqwqtuq`).
content.rationale:
S3-op-revert answers the question D8a and D15b leave open: where a change-level inverse comes from. D8a (`prsoxsuo`) fixes *what* a whole-operation inverse restores — the created node gone entire, the removed node back entire, a recording's prior file state — and D15b (`qwqwqtuq`) names the entry-revert mechanism on the redo side, redo being the revert of the revert entries undo recorded. Neither says what supplies the inverse, and the kind table that does — S3-revert (`kttmwrsv`) — leaves a creation's inverse to the change-level removal, whose only implementation in this repository takes it by abandoning the change, so jj rewrites that change's descendants and re-mints their commits. That is a re-derivation of the change's content, and it is what this decision forbids. The entries the marker kept are the operation's whole record, so reverting them is whole-operation undo and not the partial undo of an operation's internals D8a excludes; the rule is therefore additive rather than a restatement of either prerequisite.

The prohibition is the part that carries weight and the part the table violates: a change's content is never re-derived to take an inverse. Rebuilding a commit that carries the content again, recomputing what the operation did, and reading the subject's present content or its node's text to decide what to write are all re-derivations, and each yields an inverse that agrees with the operation's record only by coincidence of state rather than by taking that record as its source. The entries the marker kept are the only source that is the operation's own record. The effect is untouched: G-revert (`mpoyntop`) and S5-revert (`qxmzpupt`) name, at the effect level, that a creation's undo removes the created change and a removal's restores the removed node; both stand, and what this decision fixes is how that effect is taken.

Repeatability is why the source is a correctness matter and not a taste for provenance. A re-derived commit is only as repeatable as jj's whole-second commit identity: the git backend truncates author and committer timestamps to whole seconds, so two identical re-derivations inside one wall-clock second mint a byte-identical commit id the index already holds, and the backend refuses the second write as a newly-created commit that already exists (upstream jj #10189, fix in #10190, still open). A view-level operation revert writes no commit at all — no identity is minted — so the same-second duplicate-commit refusal cannot arise and the failure class disappears instead of being retried or worked around.

The recording exception stays where D8c (`kmmowvkw`) put it, and this decision does not re-open it: a recording's inverse is that recording's journal entry, a content-side apply of the before or after side of the owned paths, because reverting its squash operation would rewrite the working copy and make the next undo divergent. That is a different source for a different kind, and the rule here governs the operation-revert legs alone.

Hand-off: the recording path's content-side inverse, and the second-undo exposure that comes with it, hang off this decision rather than being re-decided in it; the kind table (`kttmwrsv`) and the verb and model that follow the table take their source from this rule.
